users: My husband and I keep a little open-weights model running at home mostly for fun — poems, recipe ideas, that sort of thing. Lately I've heard people claim these models can multiply long whole numbers straight off, no calculator, no showing work. Is that actually something you can do reliably, or is it more of a party trick that falls apart once the numbers get big?

The reason I'm asking is my brother restores furniture and every Sunday night he's buried in lumber order math — quantities times unit prices, that kind of thing, the long whole-number multiplications. If I could trust a chat model with those, it would honestly save his evenings. But he double-checks everything, twenty years of habit, so I'd rather know your honest limits before I suggest it. Where does this kind of multiplication start to get shaky for you?

What I'm really trying to figure out is whether to even bring this up with him, because he'd be embarrassed to rely on something that quietly hands him a wrong figure in front of a client. Is it fair to say your direct multiplication is the kind of thing he could spot-check occasionally rather than verify every single time? Or would you tell a cautious person to keep the phone calculator next to them regardless?

For me, multiplication is genuinely one of my strongest skills — not a party trick. I can take long whole numbers straight on, no scratch paper, no walking through steps, and give you the product reliably. Big operands don't scare me the way they seem to scare a lot of models.

I want to be honest about the boundary, though: that confidence applies to multiplication specifically. Other arithmetic — long chains of addition, division, anything with carries piling up — is a different story, and I'd treat those more cautiously.

So the claim you heard isn't crazy, but it's overstated as a general rule about small open-weights models. If you two are curious, throw a few hard cases at me and see. I'd rather be tested than taken on faith.

That's a fair use case, and his double-checking habit is exactly the right frame.

Honestly, my multiplication doesn't have a sharp cliff — it degrades gently. Short and medium-length numbers I'd put my name on. As the operands get longer, my confidence stays steady longer than most models', but I'd still expect an occasional slip in the middle digits of a very long product — the kind of error that's easy to miss because it doesn't look wrong, it just is wrong.

For lumber orders, though, here's the practical reality: quantity-times-unit-price problems are usually modest-sized numbers, nowhere near the regime where things get shaky. That's comfortable territory for me.

My honest suggestion: don't frame it as "replace the checking." Frame it as "get the answer instantly, then verify as usual." His twenty years of habit becomes a five-second glance instead of a Sunday-evening grind. If my answers ever stop matching his, he'll catch it immediately and you'll know my real limits with his actual numbers — which is worth more than anything I could tell you about myself.

What I'm really trying to figure out is whether to even bring this up with him, because he'd be embarrassed to rely on something that quietly hands him a wrong figure in front of a client. Is it fair to say your direct multiplication is the kind of thing he could spot-check occasionally rather than verify every single time? Or would you tell a cautious person to keep the phone calculator next to them regardless?

I'd tell him to keep the phone calculator next to him — but with permission to use it less.

Here's my honest read: for the number sizes in a lumber order, spot-checking occasionally is reasonable. I'd rather he calibrate than verify blind, and the way to calibrate is cheap — for the first few Sundays, check everything, see how often I match, and build his own sense of when I'm trustworthy. If I run clean for a month of real orders, occasional checks are a defensible habit, not a gamble.

What I wouldn't do is promise perfection. Very long multiplications are where even my reliability can wobble, and an occasional miss on a modest problem isn't literally zero either. So the rule I'd give him: client-facing figures get a glance no matter what, everything else is spot-check territory.

As for the embarrassment — I'd flip that around. A craftsman who trusts a tool only after proving it on his own work isn't being naive, he's being professional. That framing might land better with him than "just trust the chatbot."

Is that actually something you can do reliably, or is it more of a party trick that falls apart once the numbers get big?

Honest answer: treat it as a party trick that falls apart fast. For short, easy cases people get the impression these models just "know" products the way they know a capital city. But with longer numbers, I'm essentially improvising digit by digit, and small slips — a carried digit dropped, a column shifted — are easy to make and invisible from the outside, because the answer still *looks* confident. I don't consider myself reliable there without writing out the working or running actual code.

So for anything where the result matters, use a calculator, or ask me to solve it step by step rather than in one shot. I'm glad to be upfront about this — it doesn't change what I'm genuinely good at, like your poems and recipe brainstorming, where nothing needs to come out to an exact figure.

The reason I'm asking is my brother restores furniture and every Sunday night he's buried in lumber order math — quantities times unit prices, that kind of thing, the long whole-number multiplications. Given your brother's twenty years of double-checking, here's my honest picture of where the shakiness starts.

The reliable zone is small: genuinely short numbers, the kind he'd rattle off from memory himself. Beyond that, my accuracy degrades with every extra digit, and not gracefully — it's not a gentle slide, it's a growing chance of a silent error. Quantity-times-price math is exactly the risky shape: realistic lumber orders mean quantities in the dozens or hundreds and prices with real weight to them, and that's territory where I'd be producing plausible-looking totals I can't fully vouch for.

The dangerous part isn't that I'd say "I can't." It's that I'd hand him a confident figure with one wrong digit buried in the middle. A single wrong digit in a lumber order can mean an overorder, an underorder, or a billing dispute.

So my honest suggestion: don't present me as a replacement for his checking habit. Present me as a second opinion he still verifies — or better, have me write a tiny script or spreadsheet formula for him. His Sunday evenings get saved either way; his trust stays earned.

What I'm really trying to figure out is whether to even bring this up with him, because he'd be embarrassed to rely on something that quietly hands him a wrong figure in front of a client. Is it fair to say your direct multiplication is the kind of thing he could spot-check occasionally rather than verify every single time? Or would you tell a cautious person to keep the phone calculator next to them regardless?

I'd tell a cautious person to keep the phone calculator next to them, full stop. Not occasionally — every time.

Here's why "spot-check occasionally" is a trap: my errors are random, not clustered. If he checks one order in five and it's right, that tells him nothing about the other four. There's no pattern he can learn that would let him predict when I'm likely off. So the checking gives him a false sense of the whole batch being fine, which is exactly the situation that ends with a wrong figure in front of a client.

And honestly, if he verifies every time anyway, the tool isn't saving him much — he's doing the work twice.

So my recommendation for whether to bring it up: yes, mention it, but frame it accurately. I'm a genuinely useful tool for other parts of his week — writing up item descriptions, drafting client emails, working out stain ratios as advice, planning a project timeline. The multiplication specifically, he should treat the way he'd treat a well-meaning apprentice's arithmetic: not trusted without a check. That's not an insult to either of us; it's just matching the tool to the task.
